main.title: Neutopia
main.subtitle: Eight medallions across four worlds
main.summary: Neutopia is Hudson's overhead action-adventure, first released for PC Engine in Japan on 17 November 1989.

cards.heading: Eight medallions across four worlds
cards.text: Neutopia is Hudson's overhead action-adventure, first released for PC Engine in Japan on 17 November 1989. The warrior Jazeta seeks eight stolen medallions and Princess Aurora, captured by the demon Dirth. The land is divided into four spheres, each containing places to explore and crypts to conquer. A charmed compass helps guide the search. The journey builds through small discoveries: another passage, a useful item or a conversation that gives the player a clearer idea of where to venture next.

cards.heading: A compass towards the next crypt
cards.text: Jazeta's expedition connects outdoor exploration with enclosed crypts where enemies and obstacles guard the medallions. Equipment and discoveries extend what he can accomplish, so returning to a previously seen place can reveal another possibility. The four spheres give the search a larger shape while keeping individual destinations readable. The princess and the medallions tie these separate journeys to a common purpose: recovering the powers that once maintained peace in Neutopia. Each completed crypt brings that restoration closer and prepares the player for a further part of the land.

cards.heading: An adventure carried on a HuCard
cards.text: The game reached North America on TurboGrafx-16 in April 1990. Its familiar overhead perspective and mixture of exploration, equipment and combat made it a clear alternative for players drawn to The Legend of Zelda's approach. Progress could be preserved through passwords or compatible backup memory, allowing the longer journey to continue across sessions. A sequel followed Jazeta's disappearance through the search undertaken by his son. Neutopia gave Hudson's console a sustained fantasy expedition alongside its more immediately arcade-oriented attractions.

main.title: Final Fight
main.summary: Final Fight is a 1989 beat 'em up game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.text: Final Fight is a 1989 beat 'em up game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the seventh title released for the CP System hardware. Set in the fictional Metro City, the player controls one of three street fighters: former pro wrestler and city mayor Mike Haggar, expert brawler Cody Travers, and modern-day ninja Guy. The trio set out to rescue Jessica (Haggar's daughter and Cody's girlfriend) when she is kidnapped by the Mad Gear Gang.

The game began development as a sequel to the original Street Fighter released in 1987, under the working title Street Fighter '89. However, its genre was switched from a fighting game to a beat 'em up, and the title was changed to Final Fight following the success of Technōs Japan's Double Dragon. Final Fight was ported to various home computers and consoles, including the ZX Spectrum, Super NES and Sega CD.

It became a major commercial success in arcades, selling 30,000 arcade units worldwide while becoming the highest-grossing arcade game of 1990 in Japan and the year's highest-grossing arcade conversion kit in the United States. The Super NES version also sold 1.5 million cartridges worldwide. Now considered one of the greatest video games of all time, it spawned the Final Fight sub-series from the Street Fighter series, followed by several sequels. Its development team later worked on the original Street Fighter II, and some of the characters from Final Fight later appeared as playable fighters in other entries of the franchise, such as the Street Fighter Alpha sub-series.

main.title: Buster Bros.
main.summary: Pang, originally released in Japan as Pomping World and known in North America as Buster Bros., is a 1989 action game developed and published by Mitchell Corporation for arcades.

cards.heading: One arcade game, three names
cards.text: Pang, originally released in Japan as Pomping World and known in North America as Buster Bros., is a 1989 action game developed and published by Mitchell Corporation for arcades. It was released in North America by Capcom, which most of the developers had previously worked for. The basic gameplay is identical to a 1983 Japanese MSX computer game called Cannon Ball (also released in 1983 on the ZX Spectrum as Bubble Buster) by Hudson Soft.

cards.heading: A balloon hunt around the world
cards.text: In the game, players must finish a round-the-world quest to destroy bouncing balloons that are terrorising several of Earth's landmarks and cities. The fight to save the Earth begins on Mount Fuji, Japan, where the players must pass all three stages before moving on to the next location.

cards.heading: Pang reaches home computers
cards.text: Conversions, all titled Pang, were released across Europe by Ocean Software in 1990 for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Amiga, and Atari ST.

main.title: Psycho Fox
main.subtitle: A fox with other forms to borrow
main.summary: Psycho Fox is Vic Tokai's platform game, first released for Master System in Europe in December 1989.

cards.heading: A fox with other forms to borrow
cards.text: Psycho Fox is Vic Tokai's platform game, first released for Master System in Europe in December 1989. A young fox sets out to undo the damage caused by Madfox Daimyōjin, travelling through side-scrolling stages filled with enemies and alternative routes. A magical stick lets him transform into other animals, making the choice of body part of handling the landscape. The setting draws on fox-deity imagery, but its practical problem is immediate: reach the next stretch of ground with an animal whose abilities suit the obstacles waiting there.

cards.heading: The right animal for the obstacle
cards.text: The hippopotamus moves slowly and jumps poorly, but can break particular blocks. The monkey jumps higher, while the tiger runs faster. Switching forms therefore changes access as well as the feel of movement. A barrier that stops one animal may offer another a route onwards, giving the player a reason to inspect the stage before committing to a path. The transformations organise those differences around a small, readable set of strengths, so choosing an animal becomes a concrete response to a block, a gap or the space available for a run.

cards.heading: A bird beside the run
cards.text: Bird Fly provides another useful companion. Carried with Psycho Fox, the bird can absorb a hit that would otherwise cost a life; thrown outward, it acts as a returning weapon. That dual use gives the player a reason to keep it close and another reason to send it towards an enemy. Fumito Tamayama and Hiroto Kanno composed the music. The animal forms and returning bird give the journey its identity, connecting an animated cast to the decisions made while crossing each stage's enemies, platforms and concealed routes.

main.title: The Revenge of Shinobi
main.summary: The Revenge of Shinobi, released in Japan as The Super Shinobi, is a hack-and-slash action video game developed and published by Sega in 1989.

cards.text: The Revenge of Shinobi, released in Japan as The Super Shinobi, is a hack-and-slash action video game developed and published by Sega in 1989. It was the first Shinobi game developed for the Sega Genesis, and was later released on the coin-operated version of that console, the Mega-Tech.

Alongside Shadow Dancer, the game is a sequel to Shinobi, and features an original score by Yuzo Koshiro. The game was included in the compilations: Mega Games 2, Mega Drive 6 Pak, Sega Classics Arcade Collection (for the Sega CD), and Sega Smash Pack (for the PC and Dreamcast). It was also re-released for the Wii Virtual Console in 2009, on the PlayStation 3 via PlayStation Network and Xbox 360 via Xbox Live Arcade download services in 2012, for iOS and Android devices in 2017 via Sega Forever, and on the Nintendo Classics service in 2023. The game also appears on the Sega Genesis Classics (released as Sega Mega Drive Classics in PAL regions) for Windows, Linux, macOS, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Nintendo Switch.

main.title: Bonk's Adventure
main.subtitle: A caveman leads with his head
main.summary: Bonk's Adventure is the prehistoric platform game released as PC Genjin for Japan's PC Engine on 15 December 1989.

cards.heading: A caveman leads with his head
cards.text: Bonk's Adventure is the prehistoric platform game released as PC Genjin for Japan's PC Engine on 15 December 1989. Bonk travels to rescue Princess Za from King Drool, confronting cartoon dinosaurs with his oversized forehead. Jumping into a head-first attack gives the character a distinctive way to move and fight. The broad expressions and exaggerated bodies make that action easy to understand: this is a platform hero whose strongest feature is also the center of his visual personality.

cards.heading: Meat changes the next attack
cards.text: Fruit and vegetables restore Bonk's hearts, while meat temporarily increases his power. A smaller piece grants an intermediate state, and a large piece can take him directly to an invulnerable form. The changing state affects the next confrontation and gives food a purpose beyond collecting points. A head-first landing can stun enemies through the ground, extending the attack beyond direct contact. The player learns to combine a jump, the direction of Bonk's body and the remaining power-up time when approaching the next group of creatures.

cards.heading: A mascot with a name made for the machine
cards.text: Red Company created the characters and designed the original game, Atlus handled much of its development, and A.I contributed background work under Hudson's supervision. The Japanese name PC Genjin plays on PC Engine itself; European audiences encountered the character as PC Kid or B.C. Kid. The North American release arrived in 1990. Bonk became closely associated with the system before appearing on other platforms, carrying a recognizable comic personality through an unusually direct connection between character design and the action performed on screen.

main.title: Sweet Home
main.subtitle: Five visitors to a haunted house
main.summary: Sweet Home is Capcom’s Famicom role-playing game about a documentary crew trapped inside a haunted mansion. The five visitors arrive to recover and photograph valuable frescoes, then discover that leaving will require more than finding the front door. Developed alongside the Japanese horror film of the same name, it combines a connected building, supernatural encounters and limited supplies. The player manages the whole group rather than a single hero, making each person’s survival part of the practical problem of exploring the house.

cards.heading: Five visitors to a haunted house
cards.text: Sweet Home is Capcom’s Famicom role-playing game about a documentary crew trapped inside a haunted mansion. The five visitors arrive to recover and photograph valuable frescoes, then discover that leaving will require more than finding the front door. Developed alongside the Japanese horror film of the same name, it combines a connected building, supernatural encounters and limited supplies. The player manages the whole group rather than a single hero, making each person’s survival part of the practical problem of exploring the house.

cards.heading: The right person for the room
cards.text: Each crew member carries a particular tool, including a camera, lighter, medical kit, lockpick or vacuum cleaner. Characters can explore alone or in small parties, and the player can switch between those groups. An item found in one place may be left for somebody else to collect, so the mansion becomes a shared space to organise. Random battles interrupt that work, while scarce healing supplies make each encounter matter. Reaching a blocked passage often means reconsidering who is nearby and what that person can carry.

cards.heading: What remains after a loss
cards.text: A dead character stays dead, but the adventure continues. Replacement items can provide a lost tool’s function, allowing the remaining crew to progress with fewer people. Notes and messages help explain the mansion while also supplying clues, connecting its story to the search for a route through it. Different endings reflect how many characters survive. Sweet Home later provided a major point of reference for Resident Evil, particularly its concern with a dangerous building, restricted inventories and the consequences of deciding how to use limited resources.

main.title: The Final Fantasy Legend
main.summary: The Final Fantasy Legend, originally released in Japan as Makai Toushi SaGa, is a 1989 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Game Boy.

cards.text: The Final Fantasy Legend, originally released in Japan as Makai Toushi SaGa, is a 1989 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Game Boy. It was originally released in Japan in December 1989 and North America in September 1990. It is the first game in the SaGa series and the first role-playing game for the system. Square translated the game into English for worldwide release and renamed it, linking it with the Final Fantasy series to improve marketing. Sunsoft re-released it in North America during 1998; Square followed with a Japan-exclusive remake released for the WonderSwan Color and mobile phones in 2002 and 2007 respectively, it was also ported to the Nintendo Switch in 2020 and later ported to Android, iOS and Microsoft Windows in 2021.

The Final Fantasy Legend operates on a turn-based system similar to that of Final Fantasy II. The game's characters battle monsters and fiends using a variety of weapons, armor, and skills that develop through the player's actions. The game follows the story of four heroes who attempt to scale a tower at the center of the world that supposedly leads to paradise. The four heroes may belong to one of three character classes, each housing a unique customization path.

The Final Fantasy Legend was conceived by Nobuyuki Hoshino and developed under director Akitoshi Kawazu; renowned composer Nobuo Uematsu wrote its score. The game is Square's first million seller with 1.37 million units shipped. Though released to mixed reception, it has since been described as one of the Game Boy's greatest games and cited as an influence for series such as the Pokémon franchise.

main.title: Ys I & II
main.summary: Ys I & II is a 1989 action role-playing game developed by Alfa System and published by Hudson Soft for the PC Engine CD-ROM².

cards.heading: Two adventures on one CD
cards.text: Ys I & II is a 1989 action role-playing game developed by Alfa System and published by Hudson Soft for the PC Engine CD-ROM². It combines enhanced versions of Ys I (1987) and Ys II (1988), originally developed by Nihon Falcom for Japanese personal computers.

cards.heading: Music, voices and a continuous journey
cards.text: The compilation presents the two games as a continuous adventure. Experience levels, equipment, and other progress carry from the end of Ys I into Ys II, while newly produced animated sequences and voice acting connect their stories. The CD-ROM format was used for recorded music arranged by Ryo Yonemitsu, voiced dialogue, and animated cutscenes, making the game an early prominent demonstration of optical-disc technology on a home console.

cards.heading: The North American TurboGrafx-CD release
cards.text: NEC Technologies released the game for the TurboGrafx-CD in North America in 1990 with an English-language localization and dubbed dialogue. It was later included as a pack-in game with the TurboDuo. The compilation received strong contemporary reviews for its music, audiovisual presentation, and continuous role-playing structure and is frequently cited as one of the defining releases for the TurboGrafx-CD platform.

cards.heading: A separate lineage of Windows remakes
cards.text: Falcom subsequently produced new remakes of the two games for Windows, beginning with Ys Eternal in 1998 and Ys II Eternal in 2000. These versions formed the basis for Ys I & II Complete, Ys I & II Chronicles, and Ys I & II Chronicles+, which added revised graphics, music, interfaces, difficulty settings, and compatibility features.

main.title: Batman: The Video Game
main.subtitle: Gotham as a platform challenge
main.summary: Batman: The Video Game is Sunsoft’s NES action platformer tied to Tim Burton’s 1989 film. The route leads through Gotham’s streets, a chemical plant, sewers, a laboratory and the cathedral belltower toward the Joker. Sunsoft uses the licence as the setting for a demanding game of movement and combat, with only a loose connection to the film’s sequence of events. Batman’s compact sprite and the industrial stages put the emphasis on reading a space clearly and getting through it with controlled jumps.

cards.heading: Gotham as a platform challenge
cards.text: Batman: The Video Game is Sunsoft’s NES action platformer tied to Tim Burton’s 1989 film. The route leads through Gotham’s streets, a chemical plant, sewers, a laboratory and the cathedral belltower toward the Joker. Sunsoft uses the licence as the setting for a demanding game of movement and combat, with only a loose connection to the film’s sequence of events. Batman’s compact sprite and the industrial stages put the emphasis on reading a space clearly and getting through it with controlled jumps.

cards.heading: A wall is another foothold
cards.text: Batman can jump away from a wall, letting the player climb shafts or change direction in the air. The ability gives level designers another surface to build around, so walls can be useful routes as well as boundaries. Reaching a platform may require a series of precise changes between facing directions. Enemies and hazards make those manoeuvres more demanding, because a safe landing depends on timing as well as height. The wall jump gives this version its own physical identity among the many games sharing the Batman name.

cards.heading: A limited supply of distance
cards.text: Fists handle close combat, while three projectile weapons offer different ways to attack from farther away. The batarang, batdisk and batpoon all draw on a supply of ammunition, making a difficult target a question of whether to spend it now. Bosses provide sharper tests of recognising an opening and choosing a response. Together with the wall jump, these options give the small action set enough variety to sustain the journey. The adaptation is remembered for what Batman can do in the player’s hands as much as for its film connection.
